title: Parsing Trump’s Decision to (Maybe) Give Uranium Enrichment to Saudi Arabia
gist: Richard Nephew dissects the June 22, 2026 U.S.-Saudi Section 123 nuclear cooperation agreement, which reportedly abandons two longstanding U.S. nonproliferation policies: it accepts Riyadh's refusal of the IAEA Additional Protocol and creates a conditional path — via a joint economic feasibility study, with a 10-year moratorium as the fallback — to U.S.-assisted, black-boxed Saudi uranium enrichment. He argues the concepts (feasibility study, black-boxing) have merit but the concessions went too far, and warns of UAE renegotiation rights, Israeli preventive-strike precedent, and a permissive template that China or Russia could copy for Cuba or Iran.

insights.claim: On June 22, 2026 the United States announced it had signed a nuclear cooperation agreement with Saudi Arabia under Section 123 of the 1957 Atomic Energy Act, and press reports indicate the Trump administration set aside key nonproliferation policies — including preventing the spread of uranium enrichment technology — to close it.
insights.speaker: Richard Nephew
insights.so_what: Opens a US-supported civil nuclear market in Saudi Arabia while raising proliferation risk premia across the Gulf.
insights.locator: On June 22, the United States announced

insights.claim: The two concessions — a process that could permit Saudi Arabia to acquire uranium enrichment technology and permission to refuse enhanced international inspections — will worsen existing concerns about Saudi nuclear intentions.
insights.speaker: Richard Nephew
insights.so_what: These are the two specific provisions Congress will fight over — the key variables determining whether the deal survives.
insights.locator: The concessions made by the United States in this negotiation

insights.claim: The United States has accepted Saudi Arabia's refusal to implement the Additional Protocol, with primary responsibility for additional inspections reportedly falling to the United States rather than the IAEA.
insights.speaker: Richard Nephew
insights.so_what: Bilateral rather than multilateral verification means the deal's credibility depends on US political continuity across administrations.
insights.locator: On the first, the United States has accepted Saudi Arabia’s refusal

insights.claim: The agreement reportedly provides for a joint U.S.-Saudi study of enrichment economics: if it favors enrichment the United States will help build black-boxed capability, and if it does not the Saudis accept only a 10-year moratorium after which they may develop enrichment or reprocessing with U.S. blessing.
insights.speaker: Richard Nephew
insights.so_what: The 10-year sunset is the structural flaw — it converts a prohibition into a delay with an explicit expiry date.
insights.locator: Second, reportedly, there will be a joint U.S.-Saudi study

insights.claim: U.S. officials have alluded to two secret side letters accompanying the agreement, and the signed text has not been released, leaving the deal's actual terms unverifiable.
insights.speaker: Richard Nephew
insights.so_what: Undisclosed side letters are a classic trigger for congressional obstruction — a concrete near-term risk to ratification.
insights.quote: U.S. officials have also alluded to two “secret side letters” that accompany the agreement and may complicate our understanding of it.
insights.locator: The details remain unclear as the signed text has yet to be released

insights.claim: A Section 123 agreement legally requires only that the partner permit IAEA inspections, maintain physical security, refrain from retransfer without U.S. consent, and seek advance approval before enriching, reprocessing, or transferring U.S.-provided materials — a nonproliferation floor, not a ceiling.
insights.speaker: Richard Nephew
insights.so_what: Distinguishing legal minimum from policy practice explains how the administration could concede without breaking law — limiting legal challenges.
insights.locator: The specific terms of a 123 agreement are spelled out

insights.claim: The 2009 U.S.-UAE agreement became the 'gold standard' 123 agreement by securing the Emirates' commitment to forswear enrichment or reprocessing and accept the Additional Protocol as a condition of supply.
insights.speaker: Richard Nephew
insights.so_what: The benchmark against which the Saudi deal will be judged — and the contract the UAE can now reopen.
insights.locator: The primary example was the U.S. nuclear cooperation agreement with the United Arab Emirates in 2009.

insights.claim: Russia and China have been winning nuclear contracts while the United States has fallen off the map, with generous financial terms likely explaining part of their appeal and rigid U.S. nonproliferation policy presenting a complicating factor.
insights.speaker: Richard Nephew
insights.so_what: Frames the commercial motive behind the concessions — US nuclear exporters have been losing share to state-financed rivals.
insights.quote: In particular, Russia and China have been winning contracts while the United States has fallen off the map.
insights.locator: Notwithstanding this good example, the United States found it difficult

insights.claim: Since the Obama administration the United States has evaluated enrichment and reprocessing limits case by case rather than by blanket policy, which resolved deals like Vietnam's but created confusion over evaluation criteria and made restrictions look discriminatory to Saudi Arabia.
insights.speaker: Richard Nephew
insights.so_what: The precedent that made the Saudi concession negotiable — abandoning bright-line rules invites every subsequent partner to demand parity.
insights.locator: Even as early as the Obama administration, the United States changed its own preference

insights.claim: The Nuclear Suppliers Group rejected a flat U.S. prohibition and instead adopted a permissive criteria-based approach stating enrichment or reprocessing transfers should only be authorized with the Additional Protocol in place or within a similarly inspected regional arrangement such as the Brazil-Argentine ABACC.
insights.speaker: Richard Nephew
insights.so_what: The multilateral guardrail is weaker than commonly assumed, so US bilateral terms are effectively the only binding constraint.
insights.locator: The Nuclear Suppliers Group developed a more permissive criteria-based approach

insights.claim: Black-boxing shields how a technology works so only inputs and outputs are visible, and using it in nuclear transfers has considerable merit because it can give countries confidence in fuel and energy access while withholding sensitive technical detail, reducing the impetus to proliferate.
insights.speaker: Richard Nephew
insights.so_what: A reusable policy tool that could unlock US nuclear exports to states that refuse full forswearing — a potential template for future deals.
insights.locator: Black boxing refers to a set of procedures and technologies

insights.claim: Black-boxing a power reactor is far less risky than black-boxing a uranium centrifuge, because reactors need additional facilities to extract weapons-usable material while centrifuges can be immediately turned to producing weapons material.
insights.speaker: Richard Nephew
insights.so_what: The technical distinction that should determine how alarming any given nuclear export headline actually is.
insights.quote: Centrifuges, by contrast, can be immediately turned to producing nuclear weapons material.
insights.locator: There are significant technical differences in the sensitivity

insights.claim: An economic feasibility study for Saudi enrichment has security value beyond economics: if it concludes enrichment is economically unjustifiable, a subsequent Saudi decision to pursue it independently would be an obvious red flag.
insights.speaker: Richard Nephew
insights.so_what: Turns an economic study into an intelligence tripwire — a cheap, replicable verification mechanism.
insights.locator: Likewise, the idea of conducting an evaluation of the economic feasibility

insights.claim: Nephew proposes tying inspections to program content: if Saudi Arabia forgoes enrichment, the United States accepts current inspection levels but applies black-boxing to all supplied facilities and materials including reactor components — trading knowledge of facilities for a reduced inspection burden.
insights.speaker: Richard Nephew
insights.so_what: A concrete graduated-safeguards design Congress could impose as an amendment — the most likely negotiated landing zone.
insights.locator: The core principle should be the nature of the nuclear activities

insights.claim: If Saudi Arabia insists on enrichment, it should be required to accept either the Additional Protocol's enhanced inspections or a regional inspectorate providing similar confidence to its neighbors, with black-boxing as a complement rather than a panacea.
insights.speaker: Richard Nephew
insights.so_what: Defines the minimum acceptable safeguard package — anything less signals the deal has been weakened further.
insights.locator: On the other hand, if the Saudis insisted on pursuing enrichment

themes.theme: Israeli Normalization as the Live Variable

insights.claim: The entire agreement may be set aside because of Trump's renewed enthusiasm for leveraging the nuclear deal to obtain Saudi normalization with Israel — an objective the Biden administration prioritized but which U.S. sources say was abandoned in the Trump negotiations.
insights.speaker: Richard Nephew
insights.so_what: Normalization linkage is the swing factor determining whether this deal is ever submitted to Congress at all.
insights.locator: Of course, by the time you read this, the entire agreement may have been put aside

insights.claim: Israel has taken aggressive military action against sensitive nuclear facilities in its neighbors before — Iraq in 1981, Syria in 2007, and Iran in 2025 — so absent normalization the risk of Israeli-Saudi conflict over a Saudi enrichment program is greater than would be ideal.
insights.speaker: Richard Nephew
insights.so_what: A three-precedent pattern of Israeli preventive strikes is the tail risk that would reprice Gulf energy assets if Saudi enrichment advances without normalization.
insights.locator: Israel has taken aggressive action to counter the development

insights.claim: A regional model involving Israel and built on graduated inspections and black-boxing would both reduce tensions and could itself become a pathway to broader normalization.
insights.speaker: Richard Nephew
insights.so_what: Inverts the usual sequencing — safeguards architecture as the on-ramp to normalization rather than its reward.
insights.locator: A regional model involving Israel, built on a graduated concept

insights.claim: The United Arab Emirates can renegotiate its 123 agreement with the United States if another regional country gets a better deal, and its relationship with Saudi Arabia is rocky.
insights.speaker: Richard Nephew
insights.so_what: A contractual most-favored-nation trigger — the Saudi deal automatically reopens the UAE gold standard, unwinding the region's strongest safeguard.
insights.locator: The United Arab Emirates can renegotiate its 123 agreement

insights.claim: Turkey and Egypt have often been mentioned as potential nuclear competitors should a nuclear race erupt in the region.
insights.speaker: Richard Nephew
insights.so_what: Names the next two dominoes to watch for evidence that a regional proliferation cascade has begun.
insights.locator: Turkey and Egypt have often been mentioned

insights.claim: Iran's nuclear program needed no inspiration from Saudi action, but Tehran will cherry-pick from the U.S.-Saudi agreement to cement its nuclear status in future negotiations.
insights.speaker: Richard Nephew
insights.so_what: The deal hands Iran a negotiating precedent, weakening the US position in any renewed Iran talks.
insights.locator: Iran’s nuclear program clearly needed no inspiration

insights.claim: The precedent question Congress should ask is whether the United States would accept China providing an enrichment plant to Cuba without the Additional Protocol under solely Chinese safeguards, or Russia doing the same for Iran — all possible if this agreement is not sufficiently robust.
insights.speaker: Richard Nephew
insights.so_what: Reframes the deal as a global rule-setting event rather than a bilateral one — the strongest congressional argument against it.
insights.quote: Would the United States be comfortable with China providing an enrichment plant to Cuba, absent the Additional Protocol but with solely Chinese safeguards? How about Russia to Iran?
insights.locator: When the text emerges, Congress ought to give it the full scrutiny

insights.claim: Saudi officials previously said they would match Iran's nuclear program including nuclear weapons if need be, which is why proliferation concerns attach specifically to Riyadh.
insights.speaker: Richard Nephew
insights.so_what: An explicit stated conditional weapons intent makes Saudi enrichment qualitatively different from other civil nuclear programs.
insights.locator: Concerns with Saudi nuclear proliferation have been rife

insights.claim: Saudi Arabia dragged its heels for 21 years before accepting the comprehensive inspections system required under the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty.
insights.speaker: Richard Nephew
insights.so_what: A 21-year compliance record is the empirical basis for discounting Saudi assurances on future safeguards.

themes.theme: Congressional Path and Precedent for Revision

insights.claim: The agreement can still be changed either by the executive — since the president may choose not to send it to Congress over the Israel normalization dispute — or by Congress through oversight, with precedent in the UAE deal signed by Condoleezza Rice in January 2009 and re-signed in May 2009 after Obama-era renegotiation.
insights.speaker: Richard Nephew
insights.so_what: A four-month renegotiation precedent suggests the current text is not final — expect amendment rather than outright collapse.

insights.claim: The Trump administration's choices may complicate the Saudi 123 agreement and have deleterious effects on U.S. nuclear commerce more broadly.
insights.speaker: Richard Nephew
insights.so_what: The commercial irony: concessions made to win business may instead stall the deal and chill the broader US nuclear export pipeline.
insights.quote: In all, the unfortunate choices made by the Trump administration may complicate the Saudi 123 agreement and have deleterious effects on U.S. nuclear commerce.
